$comment: The fleet manifest (docs/MECHANIZATION_PLAYBOOK.md, Conversion 3) — the single source of the metro fleet, served at https://districtry.com/metros.json by the Pages deploy. Runtime behavior is deliberately unchanged: the app never fetches this file. It is consumed at GENERATION time — `generate_metro_files.py --sync-fleet` projects these entries (minus `repo`) into each fork's worksheet metro_explorers, and the weekly fleet-status workflow reads `repo` to aggregate across forks. Launching metro N+1 means: add its entry here, then run --sync-fleet + regenerate in each fork (a regeneration PR, never a hand edit). The `tag`, `landing_name`, `blurb` and `scope` fields drive the ROOT LANDING PAGE (scripts/build_landing_page.py) and coverage map (scripts/build_coverage_map.py) and are deliberately fleet-level: sync_fleet projects a whitelist into each worksheet's metro_explorers, so these four never reach an app. `tag` is the instance tag the brand spec sets in the wordmark (districtry / il); `landing_name` is the AREA a reader picks. `label` is what the apps' own switcher and handoff call the place: Illinois carries `label: "Illinois"` (renamed from Chicago on 2026-08-25) because the instance serves 89 counties and a reader sent there is not being sent to a city — `id` stays `chicago`, since it keys the instance's own THIS_METRO. `url` is what the landing page links, and since R5 they ARE districtry.com paths — which is also what the apps' own sibling-metro switcher shows, so a change here reaches both surfaces by `--sync-fleet` + regenerate and never by editing an app. `bbox` is the PORTAL HAND-OFF box, not the instance's own `metro_bbox`. SINCE 2026-09-27 IT DECIDES NO SELECTION: which app a clicked, located or searched point belongs to is settled against fleet-outlines.json (scripts/build_fleet_outlines.py, ENGINE metro-portal), and the box is only the search rows' fallback when that file cannot be read. It used to answer 'if a point falls outside the instance you are in, which sibling should be offered', and validate_index refuses a bbox containing ANOTHER metro's center. Michigan is where the two had to part company. Its TIGERweb county fabric is water-inclusive, so the state's own bbox runs west across Lake Michigan to -90.42 and swallows both Chicago's center (41.8781, -87.6298) and Wisconsin's (44.9, -89.565) — il and wi both failed the gate on it. The shipped box is Michigan's county fabric clipped to lng >= -87.60 (measured, not chosen): six western-UP counties — Baraga, Dickinson, Gogebic, Houghton, Iron, Ontonagon — therefore sit outside the HAND-OFF box and are offered Wisconsin instead, which is exactly what they did before Michigan existed, since wi's own bbox already covers them. Michigan's app still ANSWERS there (its `metro_bbox` is untouched and full-state); only the portal's tie-break is wrong, and no rectangle can fix it because the western UP shares Wisconsin's longitudes. Front-door routing reads fleet-outlines.json too since 2026-09-28, the same file the apps' hand-off reads, so the four western-UP counties this clipped box never offered Michigan now open it; the rectangle pass with its ring tie-break (scripts/build_landing_page.py's resolveMetro) answers only when that file cannot be read. MINNESOTA IS THE SECOND CLIP AND THE SAME GUARD FORCED IT, from the other side: the state's own easternmost land is -89.4834 (Cook County's Grand Portage tip) and Wisconsin's center sits at -89.565, so any box reaching Minnesota's true eastern point contains that center and fails wi's own validate_index. The shipped box is clipped to lng <= -89.58, the nearest hundredth strictly west of it — measured, not chosen. The cost is the eastern 6.2% of ONE county's width (Cook, MN; 0.0966 of its 1.5489 deg span, measured 2026-09-30), and no sibling box covers that strip either, since it sits north of wisconsin's maxLat 47.31 and west of michigan's minLng -87.60. That matters only in the fallback: since 2026-09-27 fleet-outlines.json settles every selection and mn's own outline covers Grand Portage, so the clip decides nothing a reader can see unless that file cannot be read. The rectangle cannot be made to fit — at Wisconsin's center latitude of 44.9 Minnesota's eastern boundary is the St. Croix, about -92.8, so the conflict is entirely the rectangle's corner reaching over central Wisconsin where Minnesota is nowhere near; clipping minLat instead would drop Minneapolis, St. Paul and the whole south of the state. `scope` is a short ground-truth phrase for how much of the place is covered — 'X counties' for a partial state, 'all N counties' for a complete one, 'N boroughs'/'1 city' for a city instance, and 'statewide, <city depth>' for an instance that answers everywhere in its state while going deeper in one city (New York, 2026-09-23, the first of that shape: 15 of its 33 layers answer statewide, so any of the first three forms understates it). Read by the landing page's place rows and the coverage-map legend; it says the same thing `blurb`'s prose already says in more words, so keep the two in agreement when either changes — New York's blurb already said 'across the state', which is how the disagreement was visible. ONE TRAP: the coverage-map legend PREPENDS 'statewide, ' at runtime to any instance shipping a state outline, so a scope opening with that word would say it twice; build_coverage_map.py guards it and landing_test.mjs asserts no legend row says it twice.

metros.label: Illinois
metros.blurb: 93 counties. Wards, county boards, police districts and beats, school zones, judicial subcircuits, and the people who hold those seats.

metros.label: New York
metros.blurb: Counties, towns and villages, school and judicial districts across the state, plus the city's boroughs, Council and community districts, NYPD precincts and school zones.

metros.label: San Francisco
metros.blurb: Supervisor districts, neighborhoods, police districts, school attendance areas, and the state and federal seats above them.

metros.label: Wisconsin
metros.blurb: County boards, circuit courts, wards and aldermanic districts across all 72 counties — clerk to Court of Appeals — plus school districts, cities, villages and towns, and the Assembly, Senate and U.S. House seats, and who holds those.

metros.label: Iowa
metros.blurb: All 99 counties: supervisor districts with each county's own election plan, townships and cities, school districts, ZIP codes and post offices — and the Iowa Senate, House and U.S. House seats, and who holds those.

metros.label: Michigan
metros.blurb: All 83 counties: commissioner districts, compiled by the state from the plan each county's apportionment commission files — plus townships and charter townships, cities and villages, school districts and intermediate school districts, circuit courts and Court of Appeals districts, and the Michigan Senate, House and U.S. House seats, and who holds those.

metros.label: Minnesota
metros.blurb: All 87 counties: county board districts in every one of them, judicial districts, townships and cities, school districts, ZIP codes, and the nearest police station, fire station and post office — plus the Minnesota Senate, House and U.S. House districts, and who holds the U.S. House seats. Nobody is named yet on the county boards, the judges' benches or the two state chambers, and the Data gaps panel says why.

metros.label: Kentucky
metros.blurb: All 120 counties: the county a point sits in, and the Kentucky Senate, House and U.S. House districts — with the member named for each U.S. House seat. Nobody is named yet on the two state chambers or the fiscal courts, and the Data gaps panel says why.
